# Interpreting Language Model Hidden States at Scale

- **Authors**: Jordan Pettyjohn, Mansi Sakarvadia, Nathaniel Hudson, Daniel McKenzie, Kyle Chard, Ian Foster
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-10
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10260>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.10260v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-interpretability
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-interpretability 0.40

## In one line

Makes trained lenses cheap enough to attach densely across a whole model — every layer, and residual, attention and MLP alike — and then uses that coverage to show that where a behaviour is most visible is not where intervening on it works best.

## Problem

A lens decodes an intermediate activation into the output vocabulary, so next-token predictions can be watched as they form. Trained lenses are the accurate kind and they do not scale, for three separate reasons. An affine translator costs quadratically in model width, so a dense set of them can rival the model itself -- over 200B parameters at 405B scale. Training uses KL against the model's own final distribution, which materializes two vocabulary-sized tensors per token and exhausts memory. And each lens family is built for one component type, so reading a different component needs a different lens design. Together these confined trained lenses to models of about 20B and to sparse, hand-picked hookpoints, which is what makes any model-wide claim from them unavailable.

## Contributions

- Low-rank translators, which make per-lens parameters grow linearly rather than quadratically in width
- Hookpoint-agnostic attachment: one lens family for residual, attention and MLP activations, so component types can be compared without designing a lens for each
- Subset-KL objectives that score only part of the vocabulary, including an importance-sampled variant proved to give unbiased gradients for the full KL
- A model-wide finding the sparse designs cannot reach: detection and intervention rankings over component types are negatively correlated

## Method

A lens maps an activation to a vocabulary distribution through the model's own frozen final normalization and unembedding, so only the translator is learned. That translator is parameterized as the identity plus a low-rank update with a scale factor, giving parameters linear in width and rank rather than quadratic in width; six such translators together hold about 19% of the parameters of a single dense one at typical width. Because the same parameterization, normalization, unembedding and objective apply wherever it is attached, hookpoint type becomes a configuration option rather than a design decision -- six residual, attention and MLP hookpoints per layer in these experiments. The memory problem is separate and is attacked by scoring only a subset of the vocabulary. Top-k restricts both teacher and student to the k most probable teacher tokens and renormalizes, which avoids the full-vocabulary projection but changes the objective and is therefore biased. Top-k+IS keeps the head unnormalized and importance-samples the tail from a proposal proportional to the teacher, retaining the full student normalization; Theorem 1 proves the resulting estimator and its gradients are unbiased for the full KL. A fused kernel computes each selected logit in registers rather than gathering unembedding rows, which matters because at one production configuration the gathered tensor alone would be 68.7 GB in FP32 against 0.15 GB for the kernel. Validation is a rank sweep against a full-rank tuned-lens baseline on GPT-2 Small, a matched-token-budget comparison of the subset objectives, and three case studies revisited from the literature: prompt-injection detection, multi-hop memory injection, and toxicity localization.

## Results

Fidelity is preserved at a small fraction of the parameters: at rank 64 the translator uses 16.7% of the full-rank baseline's weights while reaching 88.8% final-layer top-1 agreement and Pearson 0.984 at the final layer, 0.941 averaged over twelve. The parameter-matched rank slightly beats full-rank on KL, but inside the baseline's own seed variation, so the reading is that fidelity is preserved rather than that low rank is better. The sharper result is that **low rank is a constraint, not a compression**. The deviation from identity that the full-rank lens learns is itself not low-rank -- its best rank-64 approximation keeps only 59% of the Frobenius energy and its numerical rank stays near full -- so compressing a trained dense translator to rank 64 raises final-layer KL by 54%, and projecting it onto a random subspace of the same size raises it by more than an order of magnitude. A translator trained directly at rank 64 lands within 7% of full-rank. Low-rank training therefore finds a different solution of comparable predictive quality, not a smaller version of the dense one. On the objectives, neither subset variant dominates: Top-k gives the lowest final-layer KL and peak memory (4.8 GB against 16.3 for full KL) while Top-k+IS gives lower mean and early-layer KL, halving peak memory to 8.2 GB at matched throughput; pure teacher sampling is much worse at the final layer (0.194 against 0.067). Scale: a 482-lens ensemble for a 70B model, six times a residual-only design's coverage at the same depth, and eight optimizer steps of a 126-hookpoint stack on a 405B model across 96 GPUs, where rank 64 gives 266M translator parameters against 33.8B dense. The case studies matter more than the efficiency. Prompt-injection detection reaches mean AUROC 0.997 and, at 70B where no full-rank reference can be trained at all, catches attacks the untrained logit lens misses (ARC-Easy 0.80 against 0.68). Memory injection raises the model's probability of the correct answer 6.6x at 8B, and at a strong intervention scale where the causal optimum moves to an interior layer, the lens-selected site captures 61% and 82% of the maximum achievable gain against 34% and 66% for a final-layer selector -- it is the only lens evaluated that picks a middle layer and stays near-optimal across seeds. And toxicity: the previously reported concentration in a few attention heads reproduces, but extending the analysis across all six hookpoint types changes the conclusion, because the most effective intervention targets lie outside the attention heads examined before, and differ between models. At 8B the detection and intervention rankings are negatively correlated at Spearman -0.43 -- MLP outputs show the weakest detected toxic signal and produce the largest reduction when modified, while MLP inputs score high on detection and reduce toxicity least.

## Limitations

The paper states its own scope: experiments cover only components whose width equals the model's, so narrower ones such as individual attention heads would need a learned map into residual space that is not evaluated here; and the two subset objectives trade against each other, with Top-k biased and Top-k+IS still computing the full normalization, which the authors name as motivation for learned input maps and cheaper unbiased normalization. They also flag the dual-use risk that the same coverage exposes manipulation points. A reader should add that the 405B run is eight optimizer steps -- an execution-feasibility demonstration, which the paper says plainly, not a converged lens, so nothing is claimed about lens quality at that scale. Each case study rests on one or two models, and the toxicity correlation that carries the most interesting claim is computed over six hookpoint types, so the coefficient is a small-sample summary of an interpretable pattern rather than a precise estimate. Finally, the whole framework inherits its evaluation protocol from the tuned-lens paper, which fixes what fidelity means here as agreement with the model's own final distribution -- a lens can be faithful in that sense and still be a poor account of what an intermediate state is doing.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-interpretability**: Supplies the missing case for this archive's standing finding that a signal's detection quality licenses no claim about the effect of intervening on it. The archive already holds directions that steer opposite to what they detect, and a canonical refusal direction whose ablation recovers almost no safety. What was absent was a systematic comparison across component types, because no lens framework could be attached densely enough to make one -- and this paper's whole efficiency argument exists to enable exactly that. The answer is a negative correlation, Spearman -0.43, with the two extremes being MLP inputs (visible, inert) and MLP outputs (invisible, effective). It also warns about a second-order version of the same error: the previously published attention-head result reproduces exactly and is still misleading, because the components that were never instrumented are where the intervention works. A conclusion drawn from the components a method could reach is a fact about the method's reach.

## Abstract

Lens methods interpret large language models (LLMs) by mapping intermediate activations to the output vocabulary, revealing how next-token predictions develop through the network. Trained lenses remain expensive: affine-translator parameters grow quadratically with model width, while exact, full-vocabulary Kullback--Leibler (KL) training dominates memory. Consequently, prior trained lenses have been applied to models of at most 20B parameters and remain tied to particular component types. We present OmniLens, which applies a single lens family to any model-width activation, whether residual stream, attention, or MLP, and combines two independent scaling techniques. First, low-rank translators make per-lens parameter growth linear in model width and reduce trainable parameters by up to 98.4%. Second, Subset-KL materializes only selected vocabulary logits: its Top-k mode cuts peak training memory by up to 70%, while its importance-sampled variant retains unbiased stochastic gradients for the full KL. These savings enable a dense ensemble of 482 lenses for LLaMA-3.3-70B, providing 6x the coverage of a residual-stream design at the same depth. Model-wide coverage then reveals what single-component lenses cannot: the components where a behavior is most visible need not be those where intervention is most effective, and the most effective interventions lie outside the attention heads examined by prior lens studies. Across three case studies (prompt-injection detection, multi-hop memory injection, and toxicity localization), OmniLens reproduces key published results at substantially lower cost.
